title: Notes of Ministry - 24 - November 1974

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 24 - November 1 (2401)/Notes of Ministry - 24 - Novemb - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I desire, as the Lord may help, to draw attention to, and to incite our interest in, substance.

These are a few of many references in Scripture to substance, and the thought stands in contrast to what is unreal or imaginary. The book of Proverbs is readily distinguishable from the books of the Psalms. The deep exercises in the Psalms, I think, produce in their result what we have in the book of Proverbs, hence Solomon refers to this thought of substance.

The true thought of what is substantial is seen in the Person of Christ, as in Hebrews chapter one, where the glory of Christ is dilated upon by the Spirit through the pen of Paul, and where, speaking of the created order of things, it is said of the heavens and the earth that they shall perish. We read these scriptures and perhaps do not ponder them. When we consider how men’s hopes, and ambitions, and the fulfilment of all their desires, stand related only to what is here, you can see how vain it all is. It is so in contrast to the thought of substance.

Solomon has a good deal to say in this book of Proverbs and also in Ecclesiastes about vanity and the pursuit of the wind. It is much better to pursue substance, to go in for what is substantial, to begin on that line, because much time may be wasted in the pursuit of other things which disappoint us, and lead nowhere.
So the true thought of substance is

expressed in the Person of Jesus. You can understand how one of His disciples said, “Lord, to whom shall we go?”, John 6: 68. He touched in his link with Christ what was enduring, than which there was nothing greater, to which nothing could be compared—what he had found in Jesus. As to those who went away back and walked no more with Him, we are not told what

they pursued, but it was not substance. So wisdom is personified in this book of Proverbs, and she speaks. It is a great thing to hear the voice of wisdom. It is wisdom who says, “I love those that love me”, and then, “that I may cause those that love me to inherit substance”.

I think we may apply this section to the Lord in the way He would speak to us. What is said of wisdom a little later, as to being brought forth, when there were no fountains, before the earth was, could hardly be applied to Christ personally, but the section we read, I think, is just what the Lord would say, “I love those that love me”. That is Philadelphia. Are we in that state, beloved brethren, at this moment? Are we being maintained in it, in the sense of the love of Christ for the assembly, that we love Him, because He loves the assembly? It is not the thought that we wait until a more propitious time. There is no more propitious time than now to love Christ. “They that seek me early shall find me”. The outstanding example of that is Mary in John 20. She sought the Lord early, and she found Him. So we are told here of this

“durable wealth and righteousness” and fruit that is better than fine gold, pure gold. These things are very attractive. You say, ‘I would like as much of these things as I can have’. Well, it is good if the desire is with us to go after these things.
Then wisdom says, “I walk in the path of
righteousness”. If we are going to have these things, it is in that path that we shall have them.

If we are in the company of Christ, “who has been made to us wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:30), we shall find that that is the path in which He will lead us, “paths of righteousness”, as the psalmist says, “for his name’s sake”. We are not to be wandering. It is in conscious intimacy with Christ that we shall gain this substance. Thus we walk with Him and are subject to Him, “In the midst of the paths of judgment”. How we need to be led that way!

Paul writes two epistles to God’s assembly in a city, to lead the brethren into the paths of judgment. How important it is to have a judgment of ourselves, and of all around us; not to say that things are equivalent if they are not. Judgment is that distinctions are made, and wisdom leads in “the midst of the paths of judgment”—what for? “That I may cause those that love me to inherit substance”. Is not that attractive?
We read in the parable of the talents of the man who went out of a country and divided to his own bondmen his substance, Matthew 25: 14. That is the position in which we find ourselves.

To inherit substance is not just what is passed on verbally. It is a question of what is wrought in us. I do not know of anything more attractive than to inherit substance. People inherit fortunes and after a few generations they are worth nothing. I have no doubt that that process is going to continue. So do not let us trust in the uncertainty of riches. The Spirit of God would draw our attention to what is really substance and for substantial things we must have to do with Christ, who is the expression of them. Thank God for the apostles! Thank God for a servant like John Nelson Darby, who told us that it was the Epistle to the Hebrews that kept him out of the Romish church. Thank God for that! Suppose

he had gone there—how much poorer we would have been! Well, the apostles and others, faithful men, dealt in substance. That is what they ministered, and it is that to which I draw our attention afresh, beloved brethren—to inherit substance. It is not an inheritance quickly
gained—that brings sorrow. It is a day-by-day matter, and wisdom says, “I will fill their treasuries”.
You may feel that you are an empty vessel, but it is surprising how quickly you can be filled.

You turn to the Spirit, you turn to the Lord, and that is what He does. “Every scribe discipled to the kingdom of the heavens, is like a man that is a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old”, Matthew 13: 52. It is the bringing out there. It is such persons who can bring things out and present them, and make them attractive, so as to awaken our desire to go after them. Not only are the things attractive, but the way they are spoken of is attractive. No one could speak as Jesus spoke. Those words of grace that were coming out of His mouth made the things of which He spoke so attractive. Earlier in the history of God’s ways, there were those who heard Aaron speak, and that would be attractive because when he spoke on one occasion the people worshipped God, Exodus 4: 30–31. It is a wonderful thing to listen to a man speaking like that of the things of God so as to bow the heart in worship to God. God has people like these. There are those who love Christ and He causes them to inherit substance and fills their treasuries.
I referred just now to servants, the apostles, and others, and we have in Deuteronomy 33,
“And of Levi he said, thy Thummim and thy Urim are for thy godly one”, or ‘The man of

thy goodness’ or ‘grace’ (see note). Levi was one of the tribes. The blessing here is of the tribes, and we have a certain history referred to in connection with them. Levi was an overcomer. It is one thing to see faithfulness in men of God, but it is another thing to be in accordance with it ourselves. I think the Lord would bring us all into the sense of being of Levi. It was a very damaging thing when the idea of ‘the levites’ became official, a group of persons, a company. All the saints are levites. Another thing about Levi is that he had no material blessings—Jehovah was his inheritance. It was a tribe that God set aside in that way and He says, as it were, ‘Those persons are going to be satisfied with Myself. That is all they are going to have, and all they are going to need’. Think of having something like that in your soul! And God proved him. He has proved us, has He not? And the proving of Levi brought out something. It brought out that God’s claims were more to him than the natural. Ah! this is something that is not faced once and for all, dear brethren. It goes on and on and on in our experience with God, whether His claims are paramount.

You say, ‘My father, my mother, my brethren, my children’. Of Levi God says, “Who said to his father and to his mother, I see him not, and he acknowledged not his brethren, and knew not his own children; for they have observed thy word and kept thy covenant”. What a commendation! I feel so little able to speak of it. The divine claim through redemption and the faithful love of Christ to the church is brought to bear upon us now, beloved brethren, right at the end of this dispensation and will we let nature supersede that claim? Not Levi!
No, Levi was to teach Jacob God’s ordinances and Israel

his law. Then there was what Levi was Godward. “They shall put incense before thy nostrils, and whole burnt-offering upon thine altar”. This is what will put us in the greatest liberty spiritually in the service of God. Here we have a man, a tribe, with substance and the

invocation is “Bless, Jehovah, his substance!”. These things are what we inherit, and have inherited, and God will see us through, beloved, on this line of putting Him first. If we put His service, His rights, and His claims above all others, He will see us through.

Finally, in the verses in Proverbs 24, we have the thought of a house being built and established. Wisdom, again, is the great principle. How we need it! We need to get wisdom and to get understanding. “Through wisdom is a house built”. Solomon said the house was to be built for Jehovah and must be exceeding great in fame and in beauty, 1 Chronicles 22: 5.

Let us think about God’s house. “Through wisdom is a house built, and by understanding it is established”. God is here; He dwells in His house; “whose house are we”, Hebrews 3: 6. “By knowledge are the chambers filled with all precious and pleasant substance”. Think of the chambers of God’s house! It is a wonderful system of things that is here for God in the assembly, comprising these chambers, these holy places. “The king hath brought me into his chambers” (Song of Songs 1: 4); there typically it is the assembly’s relations with Christ, the mystery of which Paul speaks, which is great.
Well, this passage says the chambers are “filled with all precious and pleasant substance”.
“Filled”; who is going to do that? Once you get the conception in your mind of the greatness of the assembly it is delivering in its power. Many meetings are very small. What
does it matter when what is before us, what is in our thoughts, and operates in our lives, is this great thought of the assembly, God’s house? What does it matter if numbers are small?
The chambers are to be “filled with all precious and pleasant substance”. If we had made our way to Bethany on that memorable occasion, there it would be: three persons with Jesus, and

“the house was filled with the odour of the ointment”, John 12: 3. Could there be any more precious or pleasant substance than that? It was Mary’s affection for Christ, suggesting the assembly’s love in a broken day such as we are in, and yet the chambers filled.

Well, these are wonderful things to engage us, to sustain us, dear brethren, not as remote possibilities, but as actualities, because the Spirit of God is here. The Spirit of God has not withdrawn His support in any sense at all. What was at the beginning is easy to see. In the time of pristine glory in Solomon’s day the glory filled the house. We might just read from 2

Chronicles 5: 13–14 for it gives us some impression of this thought of these chambers being filled—“Then the house, the house of Jehovah, was filled with a cloud, and the priests could not stand to do their service because of the cloud; for the glory of Jehovah had filled the house of God”.

That is just the impression one had, beloved brethren, as to the chambers being “filled with all precious and pleasant substance”. The Lord has left these things in our hands. Wisdom cries, “I love those that love me; and they that seek me early shall find me … that I may cause those that love me to inherit substance; and I will fill their treasuries”. What for?
Not to make something outwardly pretentious, but that the chambers of the house might be
“filled with all precious and pleasant substance”, to His praise and glory, for His name’s sake.

I want to engage the minds and affections of the saints further with what is here, what is of God. I have read from this psalm, for in verse 4 David speaks of the house of Jehovah and of His temple, while in verse 5 he speaks of His pavilion, and of His tent. All these things are here, and they are of God. The house of God and the temple, we understand, are universal thoughts, but they are expressed in local companies. The house of God and the temple of God are expressed in this place. As Paul says to the saints at Corinth, “Do ye not know that ye are temple of God?”, 1 Corinthians 3: 16. It was not that they were the temple of God, but that they represented the thing in that place. You think of the house of God and you think of your local brethren, and so with the temple of God, pavilion of God, and the tent of God. It makes them attractive does it not?
I think the house of God would be very attractive to a lover of God, and we are in
days, beloved, when lovers of God are scarce. I speak of true lovers of God, the real thing.

Many profess to love God, but in 2 Timothy days you find that lovers of God are scarce. Men are lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, anything except lovers of God. I think the index of a man who loves God is that he is interested in the house of God. David says here,

“One thing have I asked of Jehovah, that will I seek after—that I may dwell in the house of Jehovah all the days of my life”. That is where the happiest persons are. He says, “I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thy glory dwelleth”, Psalm 26: 8. Can every one present say that?

There is a certain family in the Psalms called the sons of Korah; they are vessels of mercy, brands snatched from the fire, and they tell us in Psalm 84, “Blessed are they that dwell in thy house—they will be constantly praising thee”. That is so; the happiest persons dwell in God’s house. They are really happy. The world may not think much of them, a few sparrows or swallows, you know, that is what it says of them (Psalm 84: 3) but it says they shall dwell in God’s house and “they will be constantly praising thee”. That is what affected the queen of Sheba. She says, ‘Solomon, you have happy men’. Why were they so happy? Because they were constantly dwelling in the house. They had no other interests, and the queen of Sheba was impressed with how happy they were. How do you regard the house of God? Is every one here a lover of God? To dwell in God’s house requires a certain state.
There are three men in the Old Testament who particularly had to do with the house of

God—Jacob, Moses, and David. In his first contact with the house of God, poor Jacob is not very much at home. He says, “Surely Jehovah is in this place, and I knew it not”, Genesis 28: 16. ‘Oh! I came amongst the brethren and I was most miserable’. He says, “Jehovah is in this place … this is the gate of heaven”, and he moves on. What was wrong? It was Jacob’s state that was wrong, because whilst righteousness is the leading principle in the kingdom, holiness characterises the house. “Holiness becometh thy house, O Jehovah, for ever”, Psalm 93: 5. It is the law of the house in Ezekiel 43: 12, “Upon the top of the mountain all its border round about is most holy”. Therefore to dwell in God’s house you must be a holy person.

Many of us when we were young did not feel the meetings very attractive. We were glad to get out, like Jacob who went away to Padan Aram and spent his time there, I suppose, making money. Was he happy? Not all the time. He says to Laban, ‘You have changed my wages ten times’. He was complaining. But he had had a touch of God’s house and there was something of God in Jacob’s soul. Some of those years he just wasted on something else. But then something happens, there came the day when Joseph was born. Oh! that is a great day in your soul’s history! When Rachel had borne Joseph Jacob says, ‘I should not be here, I should be in Bethel’. So he makes a move. Joseph comes into his soul, a type of Christ, and he says,

‘This is not my place; my place is where Christ is supreme, where Christ is adored, where Christ is made everything of, and that is the house of God’. So he faces up to things with his brother and faces the matter of his associations, and he comes to the house of God. I suppose Jacob represents

the way the house of God is reached by the way of practical experience. We come to a state suited to dwelling in God’s house. Moses represents the side of ministry. He was a faithful servant in His house.

David represents a very attractive side in God’s house, because when he was a young man he heard of the ark. He heard of it at Ephratah. I suppose when David wrote this psalm the ark was in the house of Abinadab on the hill and David would say to himself, ‘That is not a suitable condition for the ark’. So he goes about to prepare a house for it. The house of God at the present time is a suited environment for the Ark. So David provides the material, and Solomon puts the material together. Thus the ark finds a resting place. Oh the glory of the house of God! From the Davidic standpoint it is most attractive; it is most delightful. You think of the saints as constituting the house of God and providing a glorious environment for the Ark.

At one point in his history Asaph went in and sat in the sanctuary provided for it, Psalm 73: 17. Do you ever do that? Take time to go in and sit in the presence of Christ. Think of the circumstances the ark was once in. The staves would remind you of the circumstances that Christ was once in, Mark 1: 13 says that He was with the wild beasts in the wilderness. You think of those Pharisees, taunting Him, trying Him. Think of the conflict of John 8 and the Man of John 8. Mr. Taylor said that is the great chapter of conflict, conflict with the Pharisees. That was no environment for the Ark. Think of Gethsemane; think of the cross, all those crowds gaping on the holy Sufferer. Oh that was no environment for
the ark!

So David provides a suitable place for the ark, a glorious environment where the ark can be at rest. He provided the material out of his affection, and out of his affliction. How attractive this is! The ark is a wonderful type of Christ. It is generally said that there is no perfect type of Christ in the Old Testament, and that is true as far as men are concerned, but there is one perfect type of Christ and that is the ark, because if you go through its history you find that the ark never let God down. At one point Moses let Him down when he asked Hobab to be eyes to them (Numbers 10: 31), but the ark went forward and sought out a resting place.
When Israel was in a low state and the ark was amongst the Philistines, the ark took care of itself.
What glory comes into your soul as you contemplate the ark, the one perfect type of Christ.

Well, that is what David wanted to see; he says, “One thing have I asked of Jehovah, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of Jehovah all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of Jehovah”. He just wanted to dwell there and let his eyes rest on the ark, typifying the Man in whom God has been made known, God in Christ. He is the Man who has made known the heart of God, the love of God, and the grace of God. Oh how good it is to behold the beauty of Jehovah! Mr. Darby says—
“There with unwearied gaze
Our eyes on Him we’ll rest,
And satisfy with endless praise
Our hearts supremely blest”.
All this is to be known now in the local assembly as we come together in the light of the house of God, the sphere where sons are
free. The bondman does not abide in the house for ever. The son abides for ever, John 8: 35.

It is the sphere of sonship, and the Ark is the central thought in the house. The One in whom the manifold glories and the beauty of Jehovah are unfolded is before our raptured gaze, we just dwell on Him personally, and then look around on the surroundings. The Lord looked round in a circuit and said, “Behold ... my brethren”, Mark 3: 34. We see Christ characteristically in the saints, we see beauty in the saints. Moses in Psalm 90: 17 says, “Let the beauty of Jehovah our God be upon us”. Look round on the beloved saints and see how attractive they are. David says, ‘I just want to dwell there, in these conditions where the ark is, and where the saints are seen in their attractiveness and in their glory and beauty as the subjects of the work of God’. They are like Christ because He is the One from whom the work of God takes character. The great end in each of us will be conformity to Christ, to the image of God’s Son; that work is proceeding now and we are to have eyes to see it.
Then David says, “to inquire of him in his temple”. It is not man’s temple, not a Greek temple, not a heathen temple, it is God’s temple. God has His temple here in this very place.
“Do ye not know that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”

That is said to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 3: 16), and so you see the saints here represent the temple of God. They are that characteristically. It is what they are in this place. That is the burden of my heart here today, to be occupied with what is of God here in this place and what
is going through triumphantly, that will never break down. So the temple is here and we are to enquire.

What do we enquire about?—God’s thoughts as to Christ and the saints. Let us learn by’ the Spirit to use the temple more, because God’s thoughts are vast. God’s appreciation of Christ is so vast! What He sees in Christ is so delightful, so attractive. God would tell us that in the temple. He would tell us of the vastness of His thoughts of the assembly. Paul says, “I speak as to Christ, and as to the assembly”, Ephesians 5: 32. Let us come together in all our meetings in the spirit of enquiry. The Spirit would unfold to us something of the vastness of God’s thoughts for the saints. How vast they are! The Psalmist says, “How great is the sum of them!” Psalm 139: 17.

Then Paul says the temple is holy and “If any one corrupt the temple of God, him shall God destroy”, 1 Corinthians 3: 17. We must be sober in the presence of these things. Mr. Taylor said, ‘If there are two companies opposed to one another, one of them cannot be the temple of God or anything like it. It is simply a deception and a mockery, and repugnant to heaven for any practising unrighteousness to assume that they are temple of God’ (N.S. Vol.52, p.433).
That is sobering. Let us then be in a state of holiness that becomes the house of God and the temple of God, for the temple of God is holy and in it every one says, “Glory!”, Psalm 29: 9.
Let us be in the experience of these things.

Then David says, “In the day of evil he will hide me in his pavilion”. Paul says to the Ephesians 5: 16), “the days are evil”. I suppose this place was never more prosperous financially and materially, and I would venture to say that it was never more evil. It is an evil day, but there is a place where we can be safe, in God’s pavilion. God has reduced us in our circumstances; He has reduced us numerically. Our safety lies in smallness. The way that Mr. Taylor put it, and there was conflict over it, was that salvation is in the assembly; salvation is amongst the saints.

You young ones, take this to heart, that you are only safe amongst the saints. They are God’s pavilion. It is a most unusual word, not much used in Scripture. It is a safe place. It represents the assembly as a sphere of practical salvation. Now David says, ‘I want to experience that in His pavilion’, “in the secret of his tent will he keep me concealed”, hidden from the world, unknown to the world. His tent is known in the local assembly. Paul set up the economy of local assemblies and he was a tent maker. It is what is working out now in the provisional time. He says, ‘In the secret of that He will keep me concealed, set me high upon a rock’, a stable position. “The firm foundation of God stands”, 2 Timothy 2: 19. Let us be assured of that. It should be in all our souls like rock. You can stand high upon it. What God has founded will never be overthrown.

Then David says, “Now shall my head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me; and I will offer in his tent sacrifices of shouts of joy: I will sing, yea, I will sing psalms unto Jehovah”. The great result is to be for the pleasure of God. It is in the tent that the service of God proceeds in this place. It is universal, of course, but proceeding in the tent. It is an

obscure, unpretentious place publicly, but what is proceeding in it is sacrifices of shouts of joy. In those verses we are really happy. We are not afraid to let ourselves go in the assembly for the pleasure of God. The sons are free; “Sacrifices of shouts of joy! I will sing … psalms unto Jehovah”. It is
not only for our blessing, but the great result is in response to God. Let us increase, therefore, as the days go by, for His glory.

How well the bride in the Song of Solomon could speak of her beloved and describe him, drawing attention to the features of beauty that enraptured her heart. I suppose that every lover of Jesus can speak somewhat about Him and His worth. Beginning at the foundation of things, they are able to say something about Him as their Saviour and Lord.

In the three passages we have read the speakers draw attention to Jesus. Peter says, “Jesus who was of Nazareth”; and Philip announced to the eunuch “the glad tidings of Jesus”. I would like to have heard as he unfolded from Isaiah 53 and doubtless from other scriptures his knowledge and appreciation of Jesus. Then Saul of Tarsus, after his conversion and after being in the company of the brethren in Damascus,

goes out and preaches “Jesus that He is the Son of God”. It shows that every real soul has a certain appreciation of Jesus as distinguished as outstanding, as eclipsing every other man, and there are many who could stand up and speak the glad tidings, and say something about how Jesus has found a place in their hearts.
So Peter is speaking to Cornelius and his household. He was sent; he had that ecstasy and was directed to the house of Cornelius to bring the glad tidings into it. So he comes and says,
“Jesus who was of Nazareth—how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power”.

It reminds you of Luke 4, Nazareth and His anointing, and the service that was committed to Him. Peter would hold all that in his heart, the great opening preaching of the Lord Jesus, quoting from Isaiah and bringing out what His mission was and what He could do on behalf of men in their need.

So Peter says, “Who went through all quarters doing good, and healing all that were under the power of the devil, because God was with him”. This is, I think, a peculiar impression of Peter’s that He went about doing good and healing. You will remember that in his epistle

Peter speaks about the things that were not present in Jesus; he says, “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2: 22) as if Peter had a peculiar impression of the moral worth of Jesus, the moral glory that shone in Him, over against every other man, Peter included. Peter would say, ‘This was not there; that was not there’. Peter would say, ‘Well, I cut off the ear of the bondman of the high priest; Jesus healed it; He was different from me; He did not retaliate’. Peter says, “Who, when reviled, reviled not again”. He would say, ‘I did; but this is Jesus; this is the Man who has found a place in my heart’.
Now he is telling it out to this gentile

household—and what effect it has! It shows how powerfully this was held in Peter’s own soul that when he told it out it had its own effect upon every one in that household, and how many there must have been. It says, “The Holy Spirit fell upon all those who were hearing the word”. So how effective Peter’s preaching of Jesus was He says, “To him all the prophets bear witness that every one that believes on him will receive through his name remission of sins”. “Through his name”, the name of Jesus; it carries all weight up there in heaven. You go and speak to God in the name of Jesus; He will listen to you; that name carries its own credentials in heaven, the power of the name; so he says, “Everyone that believes on him will receive through his name remission of sins”.

So if there is anyone who has not received the remission of sins, you just believe on Jesus, and you will receive it through His name, because that covers everything. It covers what He completed on Calvary’s cross in order that repenting sinners might be freed from their load of sin. What a name the name of Jesus is! What it is in the believer’s ear, but what it is in the sinner’s ear to hear the name of Jesus. Well, I trust everyone here knows something about the remission of their sins through the name of Jesus, through what He has effected, and how God regards His work. You mention His name, “Lord Jesus”, and it carries all the power of that name. Think of the hosts that fill heaven; we do not know about them all, but think of what the name of Jesus means up there. Think of what it was when He came in as a lowly Babe, heaven’s hosts were moved in regard to Him. Now His work is completed. He is back in heaven a glorious Man and God is pointing to Him as the One who has done all the work and the One in whom salvation is available to every needy soul tonight. What a name, the name of Jesus!
Well, it is fine to be able to say something

about it, just what you cherish in your own soul. The woman in John 4 had just a few minutes contact with Jesus, yet He found a place in her heart and she goes out and says, “Come, see a man”, ‘This Man has eclipsed every other man for me. You come to Him; come and learn the story of the glad tidings; come and receive all that He has provided for you, this water of life that will spring up in your soul, that will cause you to vibrate in a song of praise to Him who is God’.
Well now, in Acts 8 the preaching of Philip has the effect of making the eunuch wish just to go out of sight as far as this world is concerned. The eunuch comes in for the gain of the

work of Christ, so much so that he says, ‘Now I would just like to take my place with the christian community. If Jesus has gone that way, I would like to go that way too. I do not want to have any place in this world; I do not want to have any prominence for myself among His people’. He was reading the prophet Isaiah. How well Isaiah could speak about this!

What a chapter that is, Isaiah 53, covering Christ’s history here, what He was as growing up into manhood; those early years from childhood to boyhood and up to manhood. You think of all these things being cherished by Isaiah. They had not yet taken place, but he had light as to it all from God and he was able to speak about it so attractively.

The eunuch is reading about this and God is taking account of it. You know, He takes account of things that happen, of persons who are exercised, persons that mean well. God takes account of these things and He may put something in your way, or somebody in your way, just to bring in the needed touch to enlighten you in your soul as to the glad tidings. You can see throughout the Scriptures how God intervenes just to give a touch, where

it is needed, to an exercised soul. So here Philip draws near. He says, “Dost thou then know what thou art reading of?” The eunuch replies, “How should I then be able unless some one guide me?” Here is this great man, having such a place in Ethiopia, but he is not assuming anything, he says, ‘I do not know; I would like to understand this’, and asks Philip to come up and help him.

Well, these are the people that get help, humble people, simple people, who just say if they do not know. So it tells us the place where he was reading about the closing moments of Jesus’ history on earth, when He was facing Pilate, and the religious leaders, a section that brings out so beautifully the excellence of Jesus as the One “who, when reviled, reviled not again”, 1 Peter 2: 23. What features these are, what moral worth is in them, and they shone in their excellence in Jesus. We have wholly failed in these things, but He never failed. It says,

“He opened not his mouth”. He had every right to; He could have taken the place of the judge instead of the One being judged, but He accepted the place He was given, and it was all in the determinate counsel of God. So it says, “Philip, opening his mouth and beginning from that scripture, announced the glad tidings of Jesus to him”.

As I said, it would have been fine to have heard Philip unfold the glad tidings of Jesus. Philip knew them, he was given special gift to preach them, but he was able to sit down with one individual soul and he had as much joy in that as in speaking to a company, just to tell out what he knew of the Saviour, the glad tidings of Jesus, this glorious Man whom he held in his affections. What a Person He is! What a Saviour!—and how accessible. It is “the glad tidings of Jesus”, that lowly Man, whose life was so fragrant, every step of it. How fragrant to heaven were those closing moments as He faced everything, but faced it all in the lowliness of a Man who had come to do the will of God, and in the doing of it to provide a way of salvation for men.
So Jesus is preached to this eunuch, and so effectively, “And the eunuch says, Behold water; what hinders my being baptised?” Jesus went out like this; He claimed no rights at all. He just

went out, and the way men put Him out He accepted. He accepted the cross they put Him upon. So it says, “They went down both to the water … and he baptised him. But when they came up out of the water the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, and the eunuch saw him no longer”. But then it adds, “He went on his way rejoicing”. He went away a happy man. He was not seeking anything in this world, he was not trying to keep one foot in it and one foot, so to speak, in christianity. No, it is impossible to do that. You are either in one or the other.
You are either going to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season or you are going to enjoy christianity amongst the people of God.

There is nothing more blessed than to be fully committed, and it is the answer in the believer to baptism. You say, ‘Well, Jesus had no place here. What am I going to do? Am I going to have a place here? Am I going to have any of my joys in this world?’ You come to a decision and you say, ‘No, no; I am going to accept the position that He accepted and relate myself to what is of Him here’. That is the eunuch; and he went on his way rejoicing. We do not know whether he went back to a company of christians, and if he did not, I am sure he affected a few when he went back. His surroundings would be affected by a man whose soul was filled with the worth of Christ and he rejoicing in his knowledge of Him.
Now in Acts 9 it says of Saul of Tarsus, who had only recently been converted, “And straightway in the synagogues he preached Jesus

that He is the Son of God”. He too preached Jesus. What a presentation of Him it is! It is the same Person. He is still the same Person; it is Jesus, who fills God’s presence, and who will fill that eternal scene. What a Person He is, and the apostle preaches Him “that He is the Son of God”, that is, He is the Centre of another world. The eunuch accepted that he was having no place in this world. Paul says, ‘Now I will tell you about Jesus as the Centre of another world’. He had no place in this world, none whatever, but He has every place in God’s world.

What a world, that world of bliss—God’s world! It is going to be filled with persons who rejoice in the knowledge of Jesus as their Saviour. There is nothing that will enter into it but what is covered by His blood. Every family will be covered by the precious blood of Jesus, and they will all cherish Him as the Centre of it all.
So Paul preaches “Jesus that He is the Son of God”. It says, “He was with the disciples …

certain days”. It was not long, but he got this impression of Jesus. Saul of Tarsus was the centre of his own world before, and he tells of all his credentials, what he was as superior to his fellow men, all that but drawing attention to himself as the centre, Philippians 3: 5, 6. Paul brings all that on to view, not to engage us with himself, but only to bring into relief what Jesus is as the Centre and Sun of God’s world. Paul would say, ‘That is where I was, and I clung to all these things and gave myself to them. I wanted to be first; I did not want anyone to be before me; I wanted to shine as the superior one in this area which religiously claimed so much’. But then he says, ‘I have had to throw it all away’. Like the eunuch going in the water, Paul went into the water too, to dispense with all his own credentials which he boasted in and find that he was, as he says himself, “… the least of all the saints” (Ephesians 3: 8); that is, he would take the place of being the least of the company that will fill eternity for God’s pleasure.

Well, I suppose we all feel how undeserving we are, but then when we arrive at God’s thoughts about us, we are all to be clothed in the worth of Christ. That is how we appear before Him, and He could not have it any other way. He must have us entirely according to His own thoughts if He is going to have a world of bliss for His own pleasure. All this is filled out now in the assembly as an area where the saints appear in this glory, having Christ Jesus as the supreme One in their midst. May it always be true. May we not allow anything else to take His place, so that He may be the supreme One—and we shall find that it is the happiest setting we can be in. May He bless the word!
